summary: Specifies a transition mechanism that translates between IPv4 and IPv6 using address translation along with protocol translation. Its status is historic, and it was replaced by RFC 4966.

eli5.summary: A translator box lets old-style and new-style networks talk. This approach is now historic.

questions: how to translate ipv4 to ipv6 with nat
how does nat-pt translate ipv4 to ipv6
subtitle: A transition mechanism to translate between IPv4 and IPv6 networks.

tldr.problem: During the transition from IPv4 to IPv6, IPv6-only networks need to communicate with IPv4-only networks and vice versa, but they use incompatible addressing and headers.
tldr.mechanism: NAT-PT uses a border router to translate both network addresses and protocol headers, allowing IPv4 and IPv6 nodes to communicate transparently without modifications to either end.
tldr.outcome: NAT-PT became Historic and was replaced by RFC 4966, as the direct IPv4-to-IPv6 translation approach proved problematic with security, DNS, and applications carrying addresses in payloads.

today: RFC 2766 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 4966, which explains the limitations of the NAT-PT approach and recommends alternative IPv4-to-IPv6 transition mechanisms.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
NAT-PT combines Network Address Translation (address rewriting) with Protocol Translation (header conversion) to bridge IPv4 and IPv6 networks during the transition period. Unlike tunneling approaches that wrap packets in another protocol, NAT-PT translates packets directly, making communication transparent to end nodes—no configuration or dual-stack support needed on the hosts themselves.

NAT-PT operates at a border router between an IPv6-only stub domain and an IPv4 network. It maintains a pool of globally unique IPv4 addresses and dynamically assigns them to IPv6 nodes as sessions are initiated. The core assumption is that NAT-PT is used only when direct IPv6 connectivity or tunneling is not possible.
sections.eli5: NAT-PT is like a translator who converts both the address labels and the message format from one language to another, so a message from an IPv6 speaker can reach an IPv4 listener without either one knowing they are being translated.

sections.title: Address Translation Modes
sections.content:
NAT-PT has two main operational modes. Traditional-NAT-PT allows sessions initiated from the IPv6 network to reach IPv4 hosts, making it one-way from the perspective of initiation. It has two variants: Basic-NAT-PT assigns one IPv4 address to each IPv6 host, while NAPT-PT (Network Address and Port Translation) allows many IPv6 hosts to share a single IPv4 address by also translating transport port numbers.

Bi-directional-NAT-PT enables sessions from both directions. IPv6 addresses are bound statically or dynamically to IPv4 addresses, and a DNS-ALG (Application Level Gateway) must translate DNS queries and responses so that IPv4 hosts can discover and reach IPv6 hosts by name. This mode requires more complex state management and DNS handling.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to set up the translator: one-way (only IPv6 hosts can start conversations with IPv4) or two-way (either side can start a conversation, but the translator must also handle name lookups).

sections.title: Header and Checksum Translation
sections.content:
The RFC specifies how IPv4 and IPv6 headers are converted to their semantic equivalents. When translating IPv4 to IPv6, the source address is placed in the IPv6 address space with a designated prefix (PREFIX::/96), while the destination address is looked up in the NAT-PT's mapping table. The reverse translation copies the low-order 32 bits of an IPv6 address to extract the IPv4 destination address.

Because address translation changes packet headers, TCP, UDP, and ICMP checksums must be recalculated. For UDP, checksums can be set to zero if translating from IPv6 to IPv4. ICMP translation is more complex because ICMPv6 uses a pseudo-header during checksum computation, unlike ICMPv4. The RFC also covers FTP Application Level Gateway support because FTP carries IP addresses in its payload (PORT and PASV commands), which must be translated separately from the headers.
sections.eli5: When converting a message from one format to the other, the translator must rewrite the address fields and also fix the checksum (a number that verifies the message wasn't corrupted), and for applications like FTP that hide addresses inside the message, it must translate those too.

sections.title: DNS and Bidirectional Sessions
sections.content:
For IPv4 hosts to discover and connect to IPv6 hosts (inbound sessions), a DNS-ALG intercepts DNS queries. When an IPv4 host asks for an IPv6 host's address, the DNS-ALG translates the query type from 'A' (IPv4 address) to 'AAAA' or 'A6' (IPv6 address). The DNS server replies with an IPv6 address, which the DNS-ALG translates back to an IPv4 address from its pool and assigns that IPv4 address to the IPv6 host for this connection.

IPv6 hosts querying for IPv4 addresses work similarly in reverse: the DNS-ALG forwards both AAAA and 'A' queries, then translates any 'A' replies by prepending the PREFIX to create a valid IPv6 address. This DNS translation has a critical limitation: it breaks DNSSEC, because any DNS response that NAT-PT modifies will fail DNSSEC validation if the IPv4 querier is DNSSEC-aware.
sections.eli5: When a host needs a name looked up, the translator intercepts the question, changes it to ask the other format's question, and then converts the answer back. But this breaks signed DNS, because the translator's changes make the signature invalid.

sections.title: Limitations and Security Concerns
sections.content:
NAT-PT has several inherited limitations from IPv4 NAT. Topology restrictions require that all packets in a session route through the same NAT-PT router—it cannot handle multihomed deployments well. Protocol translation limitations arise because IPv4 and IPv6 have different option header semantics; not all IPv4 options map cleanly to IPv6.

Application limitations occur when applications embed IP addresses in their payloads (like FTP). Since NAT-PT is application-unaware, ALGs must intercept and rewrite payloads, which works for known applications but breaks for proprietary or future applications. Most critically, end-to-end security is broken: IPSec cannot operate across the translation boundary because it cryptographically protects the addresses, and NAT-PT modifying those addresses invalidates the cryptography. Additionally, applications relying on address stability may fail.
sections.eli5: The translator has several problems: all traffic must go through one router, it can't handle protocols with IP addresses hidden inside the message without special tricks, it breaks encrypted security, and it breaks signed DNS.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 2766 is Historic and was obsoleted by RFC 4966. The direct address and protocol translation approach proved problematic in practice due to the issues described above. The RFC remains a valuable historical reference for understanding IPv4-to-IPv6 transition mechanisms, but it is no longer recommended for new deployments. Alternative transition mechanisms, such as dual-stack approaches and IPv6 tunneling, are preferred.
sections.eli5: This approach is no longer used because it caused too many problems, especially with security and applications. RFC 4966 explains why and what to use instead.
